This February 1977 analysis covers Latin America as a region, its politics country by country and trend by trend. It was written weeks after a new American president took office. Much of the continent was then ruled by military governments, and Washington was rethinking how to deal with them.

Regional surveys like this one gave policymakers a single map of a crowded field. The analysis weighs the strength of the generals' regimes and the pressures building against them. It also captures a turning point. The new administration's stress on human rights was about to clash with the habits of America's anti-communist partners in the hemisphere.
cia-0000119590:

Warnings like this one were meant to reach policymakers before the headlines did. An austerity package could spark strikes, riots, or a cabinet's fall, and Washington wanted no surprises. The document captures that alert as it was filed. Without the country's name on its face, it stands as an example of the agency's watch work, flagging trouble whose setting the heading alone does not give.
cia-0000126890: A CIA situation report gives the state of affairs as of 1 p.m. local time on February 17, 1968, during the Tet Offensive in Vietnam. cia-0000132290: Situation Report 599 in the CIA's Iraq-Kuwait series, dated January 6, 1991, covers Iraqi political developments under a headline cut short in the record title. cia-0000135890: A CIA planning paper from 1 May 1954, now declassified, deals with planning papers with an attached briefing, the names on both layers deleted by the censors. cia-0000136290: Urgent steps at the United Nations Security Council are recommended in this June 1954 LINCOLN cable. Resolution 190, adopted on 9 June 1964, though the catalog record gives 1963, concerns South Africa and the Rivonia trial. Leaders of the anti-apartheid movement were on trial under laws that allowed long prison terms and the death sentence. The verdict was near, and the Council feared very serious results.

The Council recalls Assembly Resolution 1881 of 1963, which condemned South Africa for ignoring repeated UN resolutions and asked it to drop the trial and free all political prisoners. It notes that its own Resolutions 181 and 182 had called on South Africa to free people jailed, interned, or restricted for opposing apartheid. South Africa had rejected the appeal, a fact the Council records with regret.
un-sc-res-390: Formal action by the Council in its numbered series produced Resolution 390, which the catalog dates to 1923. These short legal texts often sit at turning points, since the Council acts when peace or security is at stake. cia-0000132490:
Dated April 4, 1960, this CIA briefing sums up Cuba's political situation for American officials. Castro had been in power for just over a year. Relations between Havana and Washington were sliding downward month by month.

A summary paper like this one pulled the main facts together in one place: the new government's course, the mood on the island, and the friction with the United States. It belongs to the steady flow of Cuba reporting the agency produced that spring. Declassified years later, it lets readers watch a Cold War crisis build in near real time.

un-sc-res-1090:
Security Council Resolution 1090, adopted on December 13, 1996, recommended Kofi Annan as the next Secretary-General of the United Nations. The catalog year simply repeats the resolution number and is wrong. Annan, a Ghanaian who had served the UN for decades, was the council's choice to succeed Boutros Boutros-Ghali, whose second term the United States had blocked.

The General Assembly confirmed the pick days later, and Annan took office on January 1, 1997. He led the UN for ten years, through wars in Kosovo and Iraq and a push to reform the world body. The brief formal text is the legal hinge of that change at the top.
stubbe-peeter-werewolf-1590:
Printed in London in 1590, this English pamphlet retells the case of Stubbe Peeter, a farmer near Cologne who was put to death in 1589. No author is named. Crowds heard that Peeter had confessed, under torment, to murders, witchcraft, and turning into a wolf by means of a magic belt given by the Devil.

The tale piles horror on horror, then ends with his gruesome execution and warnings to the reader. Such cheap pamphlets fed a hungry market for crime and wonder news. This one fixed the werewolf in English print and shaped how later writers told such tales, so it is read now as both news and folklore.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d90: John Winant, the American ambassador in London, wrote to President Roosevelt on November 2, 1943. His dispatch is Document 90 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. Winant was close to Churchill's circle and reported British thinking with a sympathetic ear, which made his letters a valued channel. The record gives the date and the two men and no topic. The dispatch is printed in the Foreign Relations series.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d190:
Ambassador Averell Harriman sent President Roosevelt a long personal review from Moscow on 4 November 1943, and it sums up what the foreign ministers' conference had shown him about Soviet thinking. It runs to several parts and mixes praise for new cooperation with warnings about hard issues ahead.

Harriman says the Soviet leaders had decided to try working with Britain and America on war and postwar problems. Molotov grew more open as he saw no united front against him. Their acceptance of China as a signer of the Four Nation Declaration proved the point, he argues. Against that, Moscow was stung by Western caution on Turkey and Sweden, and still awaited a firm answer on the Italian ships.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d290:
The British Chiefs of Staff issued paper C.C.S. 401/1 at Cairo on 23 November 1943, on airfields for very-long-range B-29 bombers in the China-Burma-India area. It answers the American paper C.C.S. 401, after President Roosevelt's telegram to Churchill asking for help in building the bases.

The British chiefs accept the American recommendations in full and are issuing orders to their authorities. Churchill has already told the commander in chief in India to give every help with the four Indian bases. One warning is attached. If the work is to finish in time, the American units and equipment must reach Calcutta by 15 January. Otherwise the deadline of 1 April will slip. The building effort may even have to stop for the Ledo road.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d390:
Louis Dreyfus, the American minister in Iran, wrote a secret letter to General Patrick Hurley at Tehran on 29 November 1943. It reports a morning call from Iran's prime minister, Mohammad Sa'ed Soheily, about the statement the conference might issue at its close.

Soheily told Dreyfus he had seen Foreign Secretary Eden that day and raised the idea of a joint communiqué built on three lines. The Allies would recognize that Iran has given them every possible help. Iran's independence, sovereignty, and territorial integrity would be confirmed, as already set out in the Tripartite Treaty. And Iran's economic needs would be considered when the peace treaty came to be negotiated. Eden agreed in principle, Soheily said, but asked him to approach the Americans and the Soviets for their agreement to go ahead.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d490:
President Roosevelt sent a message to Prime Minister Churchill on December 5, 1943, while both men were at the Second Cairo Conference. They were meeting daily, yet still exchanged written notes, which the State Department later printed in its Cairo-Tehran conference volume.

Written messages between the two leaders matter because they fixed points that conversation left loose. Roosevelt and Churchill's wartime correspondence runs to hundreds of items, and the Cairo notes belong to its most intense stretch, right after Tehran. A reader finds the alliance's two heads communicating in their own words at the moment of decision, not filtered through staff summaries or later memoirs.
frus-1944-quebec-d90:
Secretary of War Stimson wrote to Secretary Hull on September 9, 1944. The State Department printed the letter in its Quebec 1944 volume. It came three days before the Quebec Conference opened. Stimson and Hull led the two great wartime departments.

Letters between cabinet secretaries settled positions before summits began. The War Department ran the armies nearing Germany's border. The State Department handled the alliance and the coming peace. For readers, Stimson's message shows those two worlds meeting on paper. Their agreement, or friction, shaped what Roosevelt could promise at Quebec. The conference opened at Quebec City on September 12.
frus-1944-quebec-d190:
For this September 14, 1944 meeting, the editors print Eden's diary. Eden and Cadogan found Churchill with Roosevelt, Morgenthau, and Cherwell conferring about lend-lease. The visitors were welcomed as an interruption, and talk ranged over Russians, Poles, and Dumbarton Oaks until it was time to dress for dinner.

White, who was not present, adds the scene's famous line. Roosevelt delayed initialing the lend-lease committee memorandum by telling stories, while Churchill grew nervous and eager. At last Churchill burst out: "What do you want me to do? Get on my hind legs and beg like Fala?" Fala was the president's dog. The anecdote survives because Morgenthau retold it to White the next day.
frus-1944-quebec-d290:
The companion message to Chiang Kai-shek, sent September 16, 1944, over Leahy's name, hastens to inform the Generalissimo of plans for the mutual effort, particularly in Southeast Asia. Roosevelt and Churchill declared themselves determined to employ all available resources toward the earliest practicable invasion of the Japanese homeland, and were expediting redeployment after Germany's defeat to that end.

Mountbatten's operations in north Burma would continue and extend, securing the Myitkyina air bases and opening overland communications between India and China. The message asks continued cooperation from Chinese troops in Burma and the Salween armies. Success by next spring would let the Ledo Road advance with its pipelines. Mountbatten was also directed to prepare a large-scale amphibious operation in the Bay of Bengal.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d90:
Gromyko's mind was not closed on voting, the Secretary of State told the President in this draft memorandum of 20 January 1945. The draft, printed in the Malta and Yalta volume, reports two long talks between the Soviet ambassador and Leo Pasvolsky. It was prepared for Roosevelt on the eve of his trip.

The ambassador had asked many questions and seemed to be getting the American arguments into his mind. Pasvolsky gained the firm impression that Gromyko wanted to present the matter fully to his government. Speaking personally, Gromyko had even floated a distinction between discussion in the Council and formal action by vote. The draft calls that a move in the right direction, though not enough.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d190:
The new Bonomi government took office with allied blessing, this press release announced on 14 December 1944. Reprinted in the Malta and Yalta volume, the statement closes the public phase of the Italian cabinet crisis. It speaks in the name of both wartime partners.

The American and British ambassadors in Rome, it says, have stayed in close contact through the recent developments. Ambassador Kirk reports that Italy's new government rests on a majority of the political parties, those of the Committee of National Liberation among them. It thus keeps a representative character. The United States, in accord with the British government, is happy to see the new government under Signor Bonomi take office.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d290:
The cruiser Quincy carried Roosevelt into Grand Harbor, Malta, on 2 February 1945, and the President's log records the morning by the clock. The log entry, printed in the Malta and Yalta volume, comes from the official booklet of the trip. It is the plainest kind of sea record.

At midnight the ship was in the Mediterranean, steering from Gibraltar. Sicily was sighted at ten past six, and Gozo and Malta soon after. At twenty-five to ten the Quincy passed the submarine net gate into Grand Harbor at Valletta. The President stood on deck as crowds lined both sides of the channel. The ship moored at Berth 9 an hour later. The total run from Newport News stood at 4,883 miles. Churchill watched the arrival from the cruiser Sirius across the channel.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d390:
Admiral Ernest King, the Navy's chief, set down the Soviet questions put to him on February 8, 1945, with his answers. Admiral Kuznetsov had asked what had been settled about transferring ships to the Russians under the Milepost program. King answered that firm dates were hard to give. Much depended on the U-boat offensive in the Atlantic.

Deliveries, King said, could be worked out step by step, though later ones might slip. On the transfer port, Dutch Harbor might not suit. Kodiak was the second choice, and King gave his view. The memo shows sea power changing hands by schedule and training class.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d490:

Putsch explains the rules he says make small builders' work nearly impossible. He argues the agencies crush craft and choice in the name of standards big makers helped write. Carlson frames it as the builder versus the bureaucrats, the state versus speed. Car lovers and libertarians get a craftsman's case in full.
weishaupt-pythagoras-1790:
Pythagoras is the full statement of Adam Weishaupt's thought after the fall of his order. The Bavarian state banned the Illuminati in the mid 1780s and drove its founder into exile. In this first volume, printed at Frankfurt and Leipzig in 1790, he sets his ideas out as a system.

The title names the Greek sage Pythagoras, a model for a wise and hidden teacher. Weishaupt argues that a quiet circle of trained men could steer rulers toward reason and mild reform. He treats rule itself as a craft that can be studied and taught. Later writers on secret rule still treat the book as the core text of his thought.
stumpp-true-discourse-bedburg-1590:
Peter Stumpp farmed near Bedburg in Germany and died on the wheel in 1589 after a trial for murder and sorcery. A True Discourse, printed in English in 1590, carried his tale across the Channel. Stumpp is the famed Werewolf of Bedburg, the best-known such case in print.

The pamphlet says he confessed to killings done, by his own claim, in wolf form by means of a magic girdle. It dwells on his crimes, his pact with the Devil, and his hard death. English readers took the tale as true news from abroad. The print fixed Stumpp in folklore as the werewolf above all others.
worcester-witches-tryals-1690:
Four people faced the Worcester assizes in 1690 on charges of witchcraft, and The Full Tryals tells their story in full. The pamphlet prints their trials with their confessions and their last speeches on the scaffold. By 1690 such trials had grown rare in England.

The dying speeches give the book its human weight, as the condemned speak in their own voice at the end. Belief in witchcraft was fraying, yet courts could still hang for it. The record shows both facts at once: doubt in the air, death on the ground. Few late Stuart prints hold that clash so plainly.
judge-echoes-from-the-orient-1890:
William Q. Judge gave a brief sketch of his creed in Echoes from the Orient, a slim tract from 1890. The creed claims its roots lie in the old East. Judge sums up its view of God, man, death, and the soul's long road in a few short parts.

The tract was meant to be passed hand to hand. Its prose is plain and warm, fit for a first read. Fans in the United States used it as their hand book. It shows how the creed wished to be known by the crowd. The tract first ran in a tract press tied to the creed's own house. Cheap print helped it roam far on both sides of the sea.
judge-bhagavad-gita-1890:
William Q. Judge put the Bhagavad-Gita in fresh English dress in his rendering of 1890. The Gita is the famed talk twixt Prince Arjuna and his guide Krishna on a field of war. Arjuna balks at the fight. Krishna urges him to act with a free, calm heart.

Judge adds notes that read the talk through his creed's lens. He stresses the soul's long growth and duty free of greed for fruits. His version was the creed's own Gita for years. It sits apart from the plain verse takes of its day. Arjuna's doubt at the brink of war gives the talk its charge. Krishna's reply has drawn fans for two thousand years and more.
hartmann-magic-white-and-black-1890:
Franz Hartmann laid out the rules of magic in Magic, White and Black, his primer of 1890. Hartmann was a healer and a sage of the occult from Bavaria. He sorts magic by its aim. White magic seeks truth and help for souls. Black magic seeks gain and power for the self.

Chapters deal with signs, rites, faith, and the risks of the path. Hartmann warns that pride dooms the mage. The book was the chief school text of magic in English in its age. It taught a whole crop of new mages. Hartmann had roamed the world as a healer and a seeker. That broad trek feeds the calm, wide view he takes of rite and creed.
hartmann-in-the-pronaos-of-the-temple-of:
Franz Hartmann told the tale of the Rosy Cross in In the Pronaos of the Temple of Wisdom, out in 1890. The long title names the porch of the shrine of truth. Hartmann traces the band of the Rose and Cross from dim roots through the age of print and craft guilds.

He casts the band as keepers of a deep cure for souls. Tales, signs, and chief names fill the tale. The book came from the heart of the new occult wave. It links the old band to the new creeds of his day. The porch in the title marks a first step, not the shrine's heart. Hartmann hints that true lore lies past what print can hold.
kipling-the-mark-of-the-beast-1890:
Rudyard Kipling sets a wolf tale in India in The Mark of the Beast, his short tale of 1890. A drunk guest in a shrine mocks the monkey god and stamps a leper with a hot end of a smoke. The leper's touch marks his chest with a beast's print. Night past night, the guest sinks: he growls, craves raw flesh, and shuns the light of day.

His mates must force the cure from the leper at great risk. Kipling's prose is taut and grim. The tale, from Life's Handicap, is a hard gem of dread. It bites.
ashton-curious-creatures-in-zoology-1890:
John Ashton fills a cabinet of strange beasts in Curious Creatures in Zoology, his book of 1890. Ashton was a scribe who loved old prints and tales. He draws on sea logs, priest books, and fair tales. His hoard holds beasts that sit twixt lore and life. The kraken drags ships down. The sea serpent haunts a score of ships.

Each beast gets its tales, dates, and draws in Ashton's wry, rich prose. He grants doubt, yet loves the hoard too much to scorn it. The book is a joy for fans of strange life.
lavoisier-elements-of-chemistry-1790:
Antoine Lavoisier, the great French chemist, set out the new chemistry in full in his Traite of 1789. Robert Kerr turned it into English in 1790, with this title. The book threw out phlogiston and built the science on weight and proof. It was writ in a clear style that a new student could read with ease.

Lavoisier lists the true elements as he knew them and shows how acids, salts, and gases form. His balance sheet method tracks each stuff through a change, gram by gram. The book marks the start of modern chemistry, and its terms are in use to this day.
dorian-gray-1890:
Oscar Wilde's sole novel first ran in Lippincott's Magazine in July 1890, in this form of thirteen parts. The text here stands as the magazine printed it, from page scans of that print. Wilde made it longer and more soft for the book form of 1891.

Dorian Gray keeps his youth while a portrait of him grows old and foul in his place. The magazine form is more raw and more bold than the book that most readers know. It holds lines and scenes Wilde cut or toned down when the first storm broke on the tale.
mizora-1890:
Mary E. Bradley Lane wrote Mizora in the year 1890. Its full title adds the word Prophecy to the name of a hid land. A Russian woman, cast out for her views, sails north and finds a hole to a world inside the Earth. That world holds women, and women alone.

The inner land has fine schools, clean towns, and science far past our own. Men died out there long past, Lane says, and peace came with their loss. The book was the first utopia of its kind by a woman. It holds a key place in both hollow Earth and women's tales.
taylor-eleusinian-bacchic-mysteries-1790:
Thomas Taylor wrote his Dissertation on the Eleusinian and Bacchic Mysteries in 1790. Taylor was the great English voice for Greek thought of the old world. The work was the first to lay the Greek rites bare for English eyes. It helped found the grave study of pagan rites in the West.

Taylor tells of the rites at Eleusis, where men sought a blest fate past death. He reads the myths of Demeter and Dionysus as signs of the soul's path. Old Greek and Latin texts give the sparse facts he works from. The book still shapes how the rites are read today.
ibsen-ghosts-archer-1890:
Henrik Ibsen wrote Ghosts in Norwegian, and William Archer made this English version in 1890. The play scandalized London when a single club performance drew howls from the press of the day. Heredity, hypocrisy, and the sins of the fathers drive its grim, compact plot to ruin.

Mrs. Alving built an orphanage to bury her late husband's vile memory for good. Pastor Manders urges duty while she confesses the truth she hid for thirty years. Her son Oswald returns from Paris with his father's disease in his brain and body. The orphanage burns uninsured, and Oswald begs for morphine as the sun rises on stage. Ibsen shows old lies poisoning the young in one of drama's starkest works.
france-thais-1890:
Anatole France published Thaïs in 1890, here in the Library Edition English rendering of 1924 in print. The novel tells of an Alexandrian courtesan-saint and the monk who loves and converts her in Egypt. Its irony about desire and holiness made France famous well beyond France in the 1890s of his prime.

Paphnutius, a desert monk, enters Alexandria to save Thaïs, the actress whose beauty ruins men in droves. She converts, burns her treasures, and enters a convent to die in odor of sanctity and peace. The monk, meanwhile, is consumed by the desire he denied, and demons mock his wasted, burning soul in dreams. At her deathbed he confesses his love and is thrust aside as she sees heaven open above her. France balances pity for both, and judges neither, in prose of classical calm.
hamsun-hunger-1890:
Knut Hamsun published Hunger in 1890, a novel about a young writer with no money in Kristiania, now Oslo. The narrator wanders the streets hungry and proud. He tries to write, pawns his few goods, and refuses steady help. Hunger clouds his thoughts and twists how he sees other people.

Little happens in terms of plot, yet the inner life is intense. Pride, shame, and sudden joy follow one after another. Hamsun broke with the calm realism of his time to show a mind under strain. The book made his name across Europe. It is now seen as a first step toward the modern psychological novel.
james-principles-psychology-vol-1-1890:
William James published The Principles of Psychology, Volume 1, in 1890, after twelve years of work. The book founded modern psychology in America. James describes consciousness as a stream, not a chain of separate ideas. Habit, attention, and the self receive deep and lively treatment.

He writes as a biologist of the mind, asking what each faculty does for life. Famous chapters treat the emotions and the sense of self. The prose mixes science with literature in a way few textbooks match. Teachers used the Principles for decades. Volume 1 can be read alone with profit. Its chapters on habit and attention are still assigned.
james-principles-psychology-vol-2-1890:
William James completed The Principles of Psychology with Volume 2 in 1890. This volume treats sensation, perception, instinct, and the will. James also covers hypnotism, reasoning, and the production of movement. His theory that emotion follows bodily change appears in this part of the work.

We feel afraid because we tremble, he argues, not the reverse. The claim, shared with Carl Lange, still sparks debate. James ranges over animal minds, insanity, and genius with equal curiosity. The two volumes together run to nearly fourteen hundred pages. They remain a founding text of psychology and a pleasure to browse.
mahan-sea-power-1890:
Alfred Thayer Mahan was an American naval officer who taught strategy at the Naval War College in Newport. His 1890 study of sea power covers the wars of England, France, Holland, and Spain from 1660 to 1783. It quickly became the most quoted naval book of its age.

Mahan argued that command of the sea decides the fate of nations more than armies on land. He praised large battle fleets, strong ports, and trade routes guarded by guns. Leaders in America, Britain, Germany, and Japan read him closely, and his ideas fed the battleship race before the First World War.
marshall-principles-economics-1890:
Alfred Marshall taught economics at Cambridge and spent years writing the book that would train two generations of students. His Principles of Economics, published in 1890, set out the field as a calm, ordered science. For half a century it stayed the dominant textbook in the English-speaking world.

Marshall gives supply and demand their classic form, shown as two blades of one pair of scissors cutting price together. He adds tools like elasticity, the measure of how buyers respond when prices shift. His patient, balanced style made hard ideas feel like common sense carefully stated.
bohm-bawerk-capital-interest-smart-1890:
Eugen von Bohm-Bawerk was an Austrian economist and finance minister who took on Marx's theory of value head-on. His Capital and Interest, in Smart's 1890 translation, is the Austrian school's great statement on why interest exists. It mixes close criticism of rival theories with a positive account of his own.

Bohm-Bawerk argues that people value present goods above future goods of the same kind, and that interest prices that gap. Roundabout methods of production, which take longer, yield more, and interest helps coordinate them. His demolition of exploitation theories of interest set terms of debate for a generation.
blake-marriage-heaven-hell-1790:
William Blake printed The Marriage of Heaven and Hell around 1790 by his own method of illuminated printing, words and designs etched together on copper plates. The work mixes prose argument, proverbs, and vision into one prophetic book. It stands as the founding text of Blake's mythic system.

Blake attacks the tame religion of his day and praises energy, desire, and creative fire against cold reason. His Proverbs of Hell, like the road of excess leading to the palace of wisdom, still get quoted worldwide. The book remains a landmark of visionary Romantic religion and of poetry as picture.
sibly-illustration-of-the-celestial-scie:
Ebenezer Sibly published his New and Complete Illustration of the Celestial Science of Astrology around 1790, in four parts. Sibly was an English astrologer who aimed to give his art a full, grand system. Plates, charts, and worked examples filled the large pages.

Readers learned how to cast a birth chart, judge planets and houses, and answer questions by the stars. Sibly also treated weather, nations, and the fates of kings by the same rules. He claimed astrology rested on nature and long practice, not mere fortune telling. The work stands as the most ambitious English astrology of the eighteenth century.
smith-theory-moral-sentiments-1790:
Adam Smith published The Theory of Moral Sentiments in 1790 in its final form, the sixth edition of a work first issued in 1759. Smith was a professor of moral philosophy at Glasgow before he wrote on wealth. This book, his first, sets out how humans judge right and wrong.

Smith held that sympathy, our power to feel with others, grounds moral judgment. Each person carries an impartial spectator, an imagined fair witness who checks our acts. From such checks come conscience, rules of justice, and social order. The book is the moral philosophy behind the Wealth of Nations, and Smith kept revising it to the end of his life.
wollstonecraft-vindication-rights-men-17:
Mary Wollstonecraft published A Vindication of the Rights of Men in 1790. She wrote in hot reply to Edmund Burke's Reflections on the Revolution in France, which had defended the old order against the French Revolution. Wollstonecraft's answer was among the first and sharpest in the pamphlet war.

She attacked hereditary rank and wealth as corruptions that make men servile or tyrannical by turns. True rights, she argued, rest on reason and apply to all, not on birth or custom. The pamphlet sold fast and made her name as a political writer. Two years later she extended the same logic to women. The work is her first feminist intervention in the Revolution debate.
marlowe-tamburlaine-part1-1590:
Christopher Marlowe's Tamburlaine the Great burst onto the London stage around 1587 and changed English drama. Part One was printed in 1590. Marlowe, a Cambridge graduate and shoemaker's son, wrote in a new, thundering blank verse that audiences had never heard before.

Tamburlaine begins as a Scythian shepherd and rises by force of will to conquer Persia and challenge empires. He defeats kings, keeps them in cages, and marries the Egyptian princess Zenocrate. His speeches soar with longing for crowns and limitless power. The play made Marlowe famous and showed that blank verse could carry the grandest tragedy.
marlowe-tamburlaine-part2-1590:
Christopher Marlowe wrote Part Two of Tamburlaine because the first part's success demanded more. Both parts were printed together in 1590. The sequel follows the conqueror into age, grief, and death, testing how far his will can reach.

Tamburlaine now burns towns that resist, trains his sons for war, and rages against sickness itself. The death of his beloved Zenocrate breaks something in him that armies never could. He grows crueler and more desperate as his body fails. In the end the man who defied every power meets the one enemy he cannot defeat. The fall completes Marlowe's portrait of ambition.
spenser-faerie-queene-vol1-1590:
Edmund Spenser planned The Faerie Queene as a huge poem of twelve books, each following a knight who embodied one virtue. He served the English crown in Ireland and wrote for Queen Elizabeth's court. The first installment, Books One through Three, appeared in 1590 and made his fame.

Book One sends the Red Cross Knight, patron of Holiness, against dragons and deceivers with the lady Una. Book Two tests Temperance in Guyon's journey, and Book Three follows Chastity in the lady knight Britomart. Spenser invented his own nine-line stanza for the poem and filled it with allegory. Every adventure carries a moral meaning beneath its pageantry.
howells-hazard-new-fortunes-1890:
A Hazard of New Fortunes, published in 1890, is William Dean Howells's largest and most searching novel. Basil March, a figure from Howells's earlier books, moves with his wife from Boston to New York. There he helps run a new literary magazine backed by a blunt, rich dry-goods man.

Around the magazine Howells builds a wide city panorama of artists, editors, and strivers. A labor strike in the city pushes private lives toward crisis and tragedy. An old German socialist becomes the moral center of the tale. The novel weighs wealth, art, and justice against each other, and it stands as a founding work of urban realism in America.
schiller-thirty-years-war-1790:
Schiller's History of the Thirty Years' War appeared in 1790, in A. J. W. Morrison's English translation of 1846. The war began in 1618 as a clash over faith in the German lands. It grew into a thirty-year struggle that drew in Sweden, France, and Spain and left whole regions wasted.

Schiller follows Gustavus Adolphus of Sweden and the imperial general Wallenstein as the war's twin giants. Battles, sieges, and shifting leagues fill his clear, dramatic narrative. The history won Schiller his professorship at Jena. It also supplied the research behind his Wallenstein plays. For a century it stood as the standard account of the war in English homes.
verga-house-by-medlar-tree-craig-1890:
Giovanni Verga published I Malavoglia in Italian in 1881, and Mary A. Craig Englished it in 1890 as The House by the Medlar-Tree. W. D. Howells wrote the introduction to her edition. The Malavoglia are a Sicilian fishing family ruled by old Padron 'Ntoni and his faith in work and the house.

A wrecked cargo, debts, war, and jail strip the family member by member. Verga tells the tale in the voice of the village itself, proverbs and all. The book founded the verismo school, Italy's answer to French naturalism. Its power lies in patience: small blows, plainly told, until a world sinks. Howells championed it as a model of honest fiction.
fouillee-evolutionnisme-idees-forces-189:
Alfred Fouillee built his name on one striking claim: ideas are forces. His French work L'evolutionnisme des idees-forces, from 1890, states that claim in full. An idea, once held, pushes toward act and change in the world. Fouillee joined that claim to the theory of evolution.

He traces how ideas grow, spread, and reshape both minds and societies over time. Thought is no idle picture, on his account, but a real power at work. The doctrine let him link mind, morals, and social life in one scheme. French readers took the book as his core statement. It still marks his place in French thought.
spr-proceedings-vol6-1889-1890:
Volume six, covering 1889 and 1890, binds parts fifteen through seventeen of the Proceedings. The Society for Psychical Research was then near the height of its early energy. Its census of hallucinations, a vast survey of waking visions, nears report stage. Telepathy trials continue under fresh safeguards against leakage and luck.

Trance mediumship, above all the sittings with Mrs. Piper, draws long reports. Thompson's case and other trance studies of the day appear in the mix. Physical phenomena receive cooler, shorter treatment than mental ones. The society prints its doubts in the same type as its wonders. Volume six shows a research program maturing. Its files anchor histories of the field.
burnet-sacred-theory-of-the-earth-vol2-1:
Volume two of Burnet's Sacred Theory, in English in 1690, holds the two last books. The third book treats the burning of the world to come. The fourth treats the new heavens and new earth after that fire. Burnet closes with a review of his theory and its proofs.

His Earth passes from smooth Paradise, through the Deluge's ruin, to final flame and renewal. Prophecy and natural philosophy march together through the scheme. Readers of the age praised the sweep and the prose alike. The two English volumes complete his famous system. Modern geology grew partly by arguing with Burnet. His questions about Earth's past outlived his answers.
leskov-steel-flea-hapgood-1890:
A craftsman in Tula hears that English makers have built a tiny steel flea, and pride demands an answer. Leskov's tale The Steel Flea, in Isabel Hapgood's 1890 translation, follows Lefty, the cross-eyed smith who shoes the flea with microscopic shoes. The story unfolds in skaz, a yarn-spinner's voice full of twisted learned words.

Praise turns to neglect, and the fable cuts at how Russia treats its own gifted hands. Craft versus machine, home skill versus foreign shine: Leskov packs the argument into a comic, mournful tale. It remains his best loved story, a small masterpiece of Russian prose.
carnot-motive-power-heat-thurston-1890:
Sadi Carnot was a young French engineer who asked a simple question: how much work can heat do? His short memoir first came out in 1824, when he was only in his twenties. Robert Thurston's English version, issued in 1890, is the form most readers meet here.

Carnot argues that a heat engine works best when heat moves from hot to cold in a smooth, reversible cycle. No engine can beat that ideal, no matter how it is built. His reasoning gave later scientists the seed of the second law of heat science, and the cycle still bears his name.
strong-exhaustive-concordance-bible-1890:
James Strong published his Exhaustive Concordance of the Bible in 1890, after decades of work with a team of helpers. Strong was a Methodist scholar and professor. His book indexes every word of the King James Bible with its verse references.

For each Hebrew or Greek original, Strong assigns a number, and those numbers became a worldwide standard. Two dictionaries at the back give the meanings of every Hebrew, Aramaic, and Greek word in the text. Preachers and students without the ancient languages could now trace a word through the whole Bible. Strong's numbers still anchor Bible software today.
lewis-elementary-latin-dictionary-1890:
Charlton Lewis published his Elementary Latin Dictionary in 1890 as his own school abridgment of Lewis and Short. Where the great dictionary served scholars, this one served the classroom. It became the Latin student's standard dictionary for generations.

Lewis trims each entry to the senses a school author actually uses, with clear grammar help. An appendix covers the persons and places met in Caesar, Cicero, and Virgil. The definitions favor plain English over learned display. For over a century, students construing their set texts reached for Lewis first, and many scholars kept the habit for life.
gower-confessio-amantis-1390:
John Gower, a friend of Chaucer, finished his Confessio Amantis, the Lover's Confession, around 1390. It is a great Middle English poem of some 33,000 lines. Gower frames it as the confession of a lover, Amans, to Genius, priest of Venus.

Under the seven deadly sins, Genius tells tale after tale drawn from Ovid, the Bible, and old chronicles. The story of Apollonius of Tyre is the longest and finest of them. Gower's smooth couplets and moral care made him Chaucer's peer for centuries. The poem remains a rich storehouse of medieval storytelling. Kings and courtiers prized it, and fine copies survive with painted scenes.
plos-pone-0003390:
Wenyun Zhou and co-authors linked diet and a gene to cancer protection in 2008. They studied mice fed diets with balanced or low methyl nutrients. Such nutrients feed chemical tagging that can switch genes off. The typical Western diet is often low in these nutrients.

Mice on the balanced diet were protected from cancer in these tests. That protection vanished when a gene called RIZ1 was missing. So the diet's benefit seems to need this gene in place. The study ties food chemistry to one named genetic gatekeeper. Food alone, in other words, did not explain the protection they saw in the mice.
plos-pone-0003490:
Manuel Comabella and co-authors scanned genomes for multiple sclerosis risk in this 2008 study. The disease slowly strips insulation from nerves in the brain and cord. Genes play a real part, with the HLA region the strongest known factor. The team pooled DNA to scan half a million markers at once.

Their pooled genome-wide scan flagged a new risk spot at 13q31.3. A locus is a fixed address on a chromosome. New addresses widen the search for disease mechanisms. Each one may point to a fresh drug target or test. MS strikes young adults and has no cure, so each new risk spot draws wide notice.
plos-pone-0003590:
Marie Åsberg, Åke Nygren, and Rosario Leopardi hunted blood markers of stress in women in this 2009 paper. Prolonged psychosocial stress is usually assessed through self-reports. The team aimed to find biochemical markers for screening and early help. They measured a panel of plasma compounds in the women.

The panel covered interleukins, interferon-gamma, and related immune signals. Novel markers could move stress detection toward lab tests. Objective measures may catch harmful stress before it deepens. The work targets women facing long-term psychosocial strain. Stress at work is the main target group the authors had in mind.
plos-pone-0003690:
Joset A. Etzel, Valeria Gazzola, and Christian Keysers published this brain imaging study in PLOS ONE in 2008. Mirror neurons fire both when we act and when we watch others act. That finding supports simulation theory, the idea that we grasp others' actions by replaying them in our own motor system.

The authors tested the theory by sorting fMRI data across seeing and doing. If the same brain code serves both, a classifier trained on one should read the other. Their cross-modal test weighs a large claim about how social minds work, using data instead of debate.
plos-pone-0003790:
Isabelle Magalhaes, Donata R. Sizemore, Raija K. Ahmed, and colleagues published this vaccine study in PLOS ONE in 2008. BCG is the standard tuberculosis vaccine, and viral boosts might make its protection stronger and longer. The team tested a recombinant BCG prime followed by an adenovirus 35 vaccine boost.

In rhesus macaques, the prime-boost pairing drew strong antigen-specific T cell responses. Six animals received the recombinant priming vaccine in the skin, as the report describes. The strategy aims to broaden and prolong defense against tuberculosis beyond what BCG achieves alone. Monkeys are the closest test bed for human TB shots.
plos-pone-0003890:
Christiane Montag, Florian Schubert, Andreas Heinz, and co-authors linked a brain chemical to social thinking in 2008. Their PLOS ONE article concerns the prefrontal cortex, at the front of the brain. Taking another person's view is a skill tied to that region. Weakness in that skill appears in disorders such as schizophrenia and autism.

The authors measured glutamate, a key signal chemical, in the prefrontal cortex. They compared those levels with how well people took mental perspectives. A link between the chemical and the skill hints at a biological base for empathy. It may guide later work on treatments for disorders of social thinking.
plos-pone-0003990:
Daria Osipova, Dora Hermes, and Ole Jensen linked two brain rhythms in a 2008 PLOS ONE article. Brain oscillations in several frequency bands shape cognition. How those bands interact with each other stayed unclear. The authors focused on gamma power and posterior alpha activity.

They report gamma strength is phase-locked to the alpha rhythm at the back of the head. When alpha sits at one phase, gamma rises or falls predictably. Such coupling lets a slow rhythm organize faster local activity. The finding guides models of how brain regions coordinate. The paper came out in PLOS ONE, an open journal for work in science and health.
plos-pone-0004090:
Jason A. Pfister, Chi Ma, and Brad E. Morrison compared sirtuin enzymes in neuron survival in 2008. Sirtuins are seven NAD-dependent enzymes that regulate cell fate. SIRT1 was reported to protect neurons from death. SIRT2, in contrast, was reported to promote degeneration.

Their PLOS ONE article reports SIRT1 protection does not need its enzyme activity. The deacetylase function long defined SIRT1 proved unnecessary here. That surprise separates the protein's presence from its chemistry. Drug designers aiming at sirtuins must account for such effects. Readers can find the full text in PLOS ONE, an open science journal.
plos-pone-0004190:
Natalia Bondar and colleagues published this behaviour genetics study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Repeated aggression can grow out of various psychiatric disorders. The team asked what repeated winning does to the brain of the winner.

They measured gene activity in the ventral tegmental area, a midbrain hub for reward, in male mice that had won fights again and again. Four genes tied to aggression were tracked: Th, Dat1, Snca, and Bdnf. The study shows how social victory itself can rewrite gene activity in the brain, possibly locking in more aggressive behaviour.
plos-pone-0004290:
Paweł Weber, Elżbieta Kula-Eversole, and Elżbieta Pyza published this circadian study in PLOS ONE in 2009. In the first optic neuropil of the fly's visual system, called the lamina, certain cells change size and shape across day and night. These are the monopolar cells L1 and L2, plus glial cells. The most pronounced changes are the daily size swings of these cells.

The authors examined the circadian control of dendrite morphology, the shape of the branching inputs of these neurons, in Drosophila. A visual system that rebuilds parts of itself daily must be tuned by the body clock, and this study maps that tuning.
plos-pone-0004390:
Saving species takes choices about which places matter most. One guide is how much shared evolution a place holds. Nathan Swenson's 2009 PLOS ONE paper works on that measure. It deals with phylogenetic diversity, the spread of species across the tree of life. It also deals with dispersion, how closely the species in a community are related.

Many family trees used in such work have unresolved branches. Swenson asked how that weak resolution bends the numbers. If a blurry tree gives the same answer as a sharp one, field teams can trust cheaper data. If not, they need care. The paper helps ecologists know how much tree detail their conclusions require.
plos-pone-0004490: In 2009, a UK team found brief hunger helping weak flies fight. Short fasts raised living odds of weak-immune flies facing germs. The hungry flies long outlasted well-fed ones. The finding reframes defense's true costs. The test germs were gut-rod types.
plos-pone-0004590: In 2009, Walther, Albrecht, and Becker found forgetting tied to one missing enzyme anew here. Aged mice lacking amyloid β-degrading neutral endopeptidase learned better.
