plos-pone-0010990: Veal calves can pass MRSA to the people who raise them. This cross-sectional study ties human carriage of MRSA ST398 to animal antibiotic use and farm hygiene lapses. The paper maps a farm-to-human pipeline. The finding argues for tighter agricultural antibiotic rules.
plos-pone-0011090: An empty stomach makes gamblers bolder. This study shows metabolic state — hunger versus fullness — shifts economic decision-making under risk in humans. The paper links physiology to financial choice. The finding informs behavioral economics. The link matters for markets and meals.
plos-pone-0011190: A mother's schooling and status decide her healthcare. This study examines how economic status, education, and empowerment shape maternal health service use in developing countries. The paper reveals social determinants. The finding argues for women's empowerment. The empowerment saves mothers' lives.
plos-pone-0011290: Scientists can now predict where proteins receive a nitric oxide tag. This study develops GPS-SNO, a computational tool for predicting protein S-nitrosylation sites using a modified GPS algorithm. The paper offers a bioinformatics tool. The finding informs systems biology. The informed biology maps signaling networks.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1290:
The British Chiefs of Staff issued this memorandum on 18 July 1945. It came from the summit's second day, early in the British staff's run of papers. The note shows the military view being worked out before it hardened into stands.

London's chiefs had to weigh a shrinking purse against a world-wide set of duties. Their papers brought that hard math to the envoys' table. This memorandum is one of the early pieces. Read beside the American notes of the same date, it shows two allied staffs at work. They started their Potsdam labors in step, each in its own voice.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1390:
Instead of a memorandum, Mikołajczyk's paper of 28 July 1945 is a diary entry. The Polish deputy prime minister kept a private record beside his formal papers during the Potsdam period. Foreign Relations of the United States, the official American diplomatic record, prints it in the second volume on the Potsdam Conference.

Diary entries differ from memoranda in one great way: they are written for the writer, not for a reader in office. That freedom often brings candor about moods, meetings, and men. Readers can set this entry beside Mikołajczyk's formal papers of the same days and watch the public and private voices diverge. The volume gains depth from printing both, and the diary is among its most human pages.
frus-1945-50-intel-d90:
McCormack wrote to Secretary Byrnes on 23 April 1946, his last letter in the volume's State thread. He had led the department's intelligence office since its birth the previous September. It is printed in Foreign Relations of the United States, in the retrospective volume on American intelligence from 1945 to 1950.

A last paper by a founding chief carries a summing-up quality, whether the writer intends it or not. McCormack's office had begun as the heir of the OSS analysts and the seed of a State-led intelligence system. By April, that hope had passed to the central group. Readers who have followed his thread from the first hopeful exchanges of October will find this letter a fitting close. The man who built the office writing to the chief who let it go.
frus-1945-50-intel-d190:
A letter dated 13 March 1947 links two senior offices. The sender was the Director of Central Intelligence (Vandenberg). The reader was the Chairman of the Joint Research and Development Board (Bush). It stands as document 190 in the intelligence volume of Foreign Relations of the United States, covering 1945 to 1950. No CIA yet existed: a board called the National Intelligence Authority ran the work, with the Central Intelligence Group as its staff.

Letters between senior men often carried the real weight of a matter, since a signed letter put the writer's name and office behind the words. The files around it hold the answer it drew, and often the draft that came before it. Pages like this one are the bricks of the story: plain, dated, and load-bearing.
frus-1945-50-intel-d290:
A memorandum dated 17 June 1948 links two senior offices. The sender was the Director of the Policy Planning Staff (Kennan). The reader was the Under Secretary of State (Lovett) and Secretary of State Marshall. The State Department prints it as document 290 in Foreign Relations of the United States, in the intelligence volume for 1945 to 1950. The CIA was in its first year, and the Council was taking up covert action for the first time.

Memos like this one did the quiet work of the system. They carried facts, advice, and requests from one office to the desk that could act on them. The note's brevity hides its weight: men at this level did not write to each other for practice. For a reader of the period, the piece fills one link in the chain between the war's end and the settled Cold War system.
frus-1945-50-intel-d390:
On 25 July 1949, the Executive Secretary (Souers) sent a memorandum to the National Security Council. The editors of Foreign Relations of the United States placed it as document 390 in the 1945 to 1950 intelligence volume. By then the Dulles Report was months old, and the argument had moved to putting its advice into practice.

The memo form let a staff officer speak straight to a chief: here is the point, here are the facts, here is what is asked. A reader can watch the system think on paper: a fact here, a doubt there, a choice asked for at the end. The FRUS editors kept it because the chain of choices is not whole without it.
frus-1861-d90:
Charles Francis Adams wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 11 October 1861. The dispatch is document 90 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

By mid October, Adams had held his post for five months of war. His reports kept their even tone through praise and blame in the press. The letter shows the worth of a steady man in a post where a hot word could cost a country its cause. A hot word in London could have undone a year of care in a single week. Steady men in hot posts are the quiet heroes of this whole record.
frus-1861-d190:
Mr. Stockton wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 14 September 1861. The dispatch is document 190 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Stockton's September report answers, across a long gap, the April letter from Seward. The record gives no post for him in either heading. His page joins the file as a lone report, its value lying in its date and its place in the year's run. A lone report still earns its place, as one dated point in the year's wide record. One dated point, honestly kept, can anchor a whole chapter of the year's tale.
frus-1861-d290:
Writing on 25 July 1861, Mr. Harvey sent his report to Secretary of State William H. Seward. It was printed as Document 290 in the foreign affairs papers sent to the two houses of Congress. The date falls in the first summer of the Civil War, when the Union fought to keep foreign powers from backing the South.

Such reports fed the facts and rumors together into one desk in Washington, week by week. Its worth grows in context, as one link in a chain of letters that kept the peace with Europe. Foreign Relations of the United States, the official record series, is where the full exchange can be traced.
frus-1862-d90:
A letter home from Charles Francis Adams, dated 3 July 1862, landed on Seward's desk. It was printed as Document 90 in Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs for 1862. It belongs to the summer of 1862, the war's second year, when keeping Europe out of the war was a core task for Washington.

Such reports fed the facts and rumors together into one desk in Washington, week by week. For students of the war, the value lies in the sequence: one dated step in a long exchange. The Foreign Relations series, kept by the State Department's Office of the Historian, preserves the full run.
frus-1862-d190:
Two Seward letters to London bear the date 18 November 1862, and the first is Document 190 in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. Charles Francis Adams, the American minister to Britain, received it from Secretary of State William H. Seward.

Mid-November mail crossed an Atlantic growing calmer on the war question, since Britain had declined the French truce plan. Other business filled the gap: Confederate ships in British yards, trade, and the treatment of Union vessels. This dispatch is part of the shift from crisis management to the daily grind of holding neutrality in place. Earl Russell, the British foreign secretary, was the minister Adams dealt with most in London.
frus-1862-d290:
On 21 June 1862 Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote again to William L. Dayton in Paris, in a dispatch printed as Document 290 of the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. Three letters in two days mark a heavy mail.

A steamer's sailing explains such clusters: the Department cleared pending business before the bag closed. Seward's June letters to Dayton went out while Stuart handled Britain's legation in Washington and Lee prepared to strike near Richmond. The cluster shows a government working several channels at once, each letter a small part of a larger design. France's Mexican venture shared the court's attention with the American war all year.
frus-1862-d390:
Two Seward dispatches to Simon Cameron are dated 6 September 1862, and the first is Document 390 in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. Cameron was the American minister in Russia, at St. Petersburg.

Seward wrote six days after Bull Run, with Lee entering Maryland. His September mail to St. Petersburg carried Washington's account of a hard month to the court least likely to doubt it. The pair of letters that day shows the Department keeping even its quietest channel current in a crisis week. The legation's quiet year was the exception in a volume full of friction. Cameron, a Pennsylvania political chief, had run the War Department before going to Russia.
frus-1862-d490:
Dated 16 March 1862, this report from James Shepherd Pike at The Hague reached Secretary of State William H. Seward out of strict order in the printed file. It is Document 490 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs.

The volume's editors grouped letters as they were received and printed, so a Hague report of mid-March can sit behind one dated days later. Pike's subject in those weeks was the Netherlands itself: its ministry's caution, its merchants' losses, and its colonial stake in the Caribbean. His dispatch adds one more layer to the Dutch record for March, a month in which Seward wrote to The Hague four times. The file's density is the point: Washington watched even friendly small powers closely.
frus-1862-d590:
On 7 June 1862 Secretary of State William H. Seward addressed this instruction to Thomas Corwin in Mexico City. It is Document 590 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, accompanying the annual message.

June orders to Mexico went out as the armies closed on Richmond, and Washington's mind was necessarily divided. Seward still kept the Mexican brief exact: support for the republic's independence, protest against the French design, and no step that risked war with France. Corwin, on the ground, had to make that limited brief feel like friendship to a government under invasion. The instruction is one of the year's clearest statements of how the Union rationed its strength abroad while its own survival was undecided.
frus-1862-d690: Dated 20 March 1862, this dispatch from a Mr. De Long went to Secretary of State William H. Seward. It is document 690 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1862, the last of his run of letters that winter. The title and record name him and the date only, so his post and subject stay unstated here.
frus-1863p1-d90:
On 24 February 1863, Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London. The letter is document 90 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863. It opens a three-day run of Seward letters in the file.

Seward's late-February sheets set the brief anew as spring neared. The war at home was stuck in winter mud, and the talks abroad moved by small steps. His letters told Adams which claims to press and which to let rest. This one begins that run, a sign that Washington meant to keep its London hand tight as the season turned.
frus-1863p1-d190:
Reporting on 7 May 1863, Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London, wrote home to Secretary of State William H. Seward. The report is document 190 in the 1863 diplomatic papers. The document comes from the Foreign Relations of the United States, the government's own published record of Civil War diplomacy. It was one of 4 letters between the same men dated that day.

The CSS Alabama, built in a British yard, had escaped to sea in 1862 and was burning Union merchant ships. London's handling of such ships hung over every report Adams sent home. Alone it settles little; in the run of the volume it helps explain why Britain stayed out of the American war.
frus-1863p1-d290:
A dispatch dated 10 September 1863 carried news from Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London, to Secretary of State William H. Seward in Washington. It is document 290 in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume. The letter is printed in Foreign Relations of the United States, the official series that publishes American diplomatic papers.

Union wins at Gettysburg and Vicksburg in early July 1863 weakened the case for aiding the South. British leaders grew more careful, and Adams's post grew a little less tense. Historians still mine this correspondence for the inside story of Anglo-American relations during the war.
frus-1863p1-d390:
One entry in the running Washington exchange, this note from Secretary of State William H. Seward to Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington, is dated 11 February 1863. It stands as document 390 of the 1863 diplomatic papers. The text is preserved in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume, which gathered the year's diplomatic mail for Congress and the public.

Read together, these letters trace a slow cooling of the crisis mood of 1861 and 1862. Recognition of the South grew less likely with each month the channel stayed open. Alone it settles little; in the run of the volume it helps explain why Britain stayed out of the American war.
frus-1863p1-d490:
Under the date 4 May 1863, the record holds a letter from Lord Lyons, Britain's envoy in Washington to Secretary William H. Seward. Such notes moved by hand between the State Department and the British legation, a few streets apart in wartime Washington. Britain had not taken sides in the American war, and holding that line was the daily work of this mail.

None of these letters worked alone. Read in sequence, they show two governments testing each other's limits while both, in the end, avoided a second war. Trade ran through the whole exchange. British mills wanted Southern cotton, while Union officials watched every cargo for war goods bound to the South. The volume's editors printed it without comment; its meaning comes from the company it keeps in the file.
frus-1863p1-d590:
Secretary William H. Seward directed a letter to Lord Lyons, the British minister in Washington on 17 July 1863. Behind the formal phrases stood a live question: would Britain stay neutral, or step into the American war? The State Department later published the letter in its 1863 foreign affairs volume, laid before Congress with the President's message.

Letters like this one were the tools of a quiet contest. The Union meant to keep Britain out of the war, and it made that case note by note. British subjects caught up in the war filled many pages: men arrested, goods seized, and claims for losses that London took up with Washington. Kept with the rest of the 1863 papers, it helps the full story of wartime diplomacy stay traceable, letter by letter.
frus-1863p1-d690:
William H. Seward wrote once more to Lord Lyons on 11 November 1863. Lyons, the British minister in Washington, was his most frequent foreign contact that fall. The letter is document 690 in Foreign Relations of the United States for 1863.

Three notes in this run bear the same date, which tells its own story about the load of work. The Union wanted trade kept open and the South kept isolated. Britain wanted its ships and goods kept safe. Seward's mail walked that line in short, firm steps. This dispatch is one such step, and its worth lies in the full sequence it belongs to.
plos-pbio-0020090:
Frances Crawford, Eric Huseby, Janice White, and co-workers built a screening tool for T cells in PLOS Biology in 2004. T cells react to peptide fragments shown by MHC proteins on cell surfaces. The team made a display library of such pairs to fish out reactive T cells, including rare ones that react to the body's own tissues.

Some T cells attack self tissue and drive autoimmune disease, yet they are hard to find and study. A library that presents many peptide-MHC pairs at once makes that search practical. The tool can reveal what these cells see and how strongly they respond. That knowledge may help design treatments that calm only the harmful cells and spare the rest.
plos-pbio-0020290:
Elizabeth A. Hadly, Uma Ramakrishnan, Yvonne L. Chan, and their team read climate history from ancient DNA in PLOS Biology in 2004. They used DNA from old specimens, paired with family-tree timing methods. With them, they tracked how animal populations rose and fell as the climate shifted.

Their approach, called phylochronology, turns fossils and museum samples into a time series of genetic change. It showed population crashes and rebounds tied to warming and cooling. That record is a guide for the present. Species facing rapid warming now may follow paths seen in the data. The paper helped launch a field that reads the past to forecast the fate of wildlife.
plos-pone-0000090:
Tobias Kalisch, Claudia Wilimzig, Nadine Kleibel, and their team studied handedness across age in PLOS ONE in 2006. Most right-handed people do skilled tasks far better with the right hand. The team found that this gap between hands shrinks in older adults, a change called attenuation of hand superiority.

The dominant hand loses its edge as age advances, likely because the brain and body systems that keep it special wear unevenly. That finding matters for stroke care and for testing older patients. A smaller gap is normal in old age, so doctors should not read it as damage by itself. The study gives aging research a clean baseline for a basic human trait.
plos-pone-0000190:
Akihiro Horii, Xiumei Wang, Fabrizio Gelain, and colleagues published this biomaterials paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. It follows up on designer peptide nanofiber scaffolds, self-assembling protein fibers used to grow cells in three dimensions. This time the cells are osteoblasts, the builders of bone, and the title reports the scaffolds strongly boost their growth, maturation, and 3-D migration.

A scaffold that bone cells thrive on is a candidate material for repairing bone. The authors measure how much better the osteoblasts do on the designer fibers. The work is part of a push toward lab-made matrices that the body treats like its own tissue scaffolding.
plos-pone-0000290:
Rayna I. Kraeva, Dragomir B. Krastev, Assen Roguev, and colleagues published this molecular biology paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. When a gene is transcribed, its message can form duplexes, paired strands, with DNA or with other RNA. The authors show that the stability of mRNA/DNA and DNA/DNA duplexes affects how much mRNA gets transcribed.

Stability is set by sequence, so the DNA code itself can throttle its own reading. The finding adds a physical layer to gene regulation, beyond proteins that switch genes on and off. It matters for predicting expression from sequence, a basic task in genomics.
plos-pone-0000390:
Philipp Leucht and colleagues examined how bone heals, in a 2007 PLOS ONE study of skeletal regeneration. Healing bone must sense physical forces, a process called mechanotransduction, where cells convert pressure and strain into chemical signals. The work centers on FAK, a protein that helps cells register those forces.

Broken and regrowing bone is loaded and stressed as an animal moves, and cells use that input to shape the repair. If FAK carries much of that signal, then blocking or boosting it could change how well bone mends. The study speaks to fracture care and to the design of implants and scaffolds that work with the body's own repair signals.
plos-pone-0000490:
Dan Zhou and colleagues bred fruit flies to survive air with almost no oxygen, reporting in PLOS ONE in 2007. The experiment used experimental selection: over generations, only flies that tolerated an extremely low oxygen environment reproduced. Drosophila became a test of how fast evolution can push a hard physiological limit.

Surviving near-zero oxygen matters medically, since human tissues face oxygen shortage in stroke, heart attack, and altitude sickness. Flies that crack the problem reveal which genes and pathways can be tuned. Selection experiments of this kind show evolution working in real time, on a trait with clear survival stakes.
plos-pone-0000590:
Johannes J. Le Roux and colleagues documented a plant clone that conquered the world, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper titled Super-Genotype. Against the odds of nature, a single genotype has spread across the globe. Vast numbers of plants are genetically one individual. They spread by cuttings and fragments rather than seed.

A clone that succeeds everywhere challenges the idea that genetic diversity is required for success. Such super-genotypes are often invasive species, where one tough genotype exploits many environments. Understanding how a clone wins helps predict and manage invasions, and it tests evolutionary theory's assumptions about sex and variation.
plos-pone-0000690:
Ryan J. Mailloux, Robin Bériault, Joseph Lemire and co-authors found a novel twist in one of metabolism's oldest pathways, for PLOS ONE in 2007. The tricarboxylic acid cycle, or TCA cycle, runs in all organisms that use oxygen. It supplies building blocks for growth and the reducing factors NADH and FADH2 that drive energy generation.

Textbooks treat the cycle as a closed loop of chemistry. The authors show this network is also an integral part of something more, in their words a novel twist on the ancient system. Discoveries inside such a well-mapped pathway are rare. They remind readers that even core metabolism still holds surprises.
plos-pone-0000790:
Fabien Burki, Kamran Shalchian-Tabrizi, Marianne Minge and co-authors redrew the top branches of the family tree of complex cells. Sorting out how eukaryotes, the group that holds animals, plants, fungi, and many microbes, are related is a long-running hard problem. Gene data had lately sorted all of them into five or six large supergroups. That scheme was the view being tested.

Using many genes at once, a method called phylogenomics, the team found the supergroups needed reshuffling. Some groups merged, and some ties between groups changed. Moves at this level shift whole kingdoms of life. The study shows how fast rich gene data can upset trees built from one or two genes.
plos-pone-0000890:
Simon Lacey, Andrew Peters and K. Sathian tested whether recognizing an object by sight and by touch depends on viewpoint, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Earlier work had suggested that both visual and touch based recognition suffer when an object is turned. Those studies, though, used objects stretched along one axis, which may have skewed the result.

Lacey and co-authors revisited the question with that flaw in mind. Their title gives the direction of the work: cross-modal recognition, matching what is seen with what is felt, can hold up across viewpoints. The finding matters for how we think the brain stores shape. It suggests shape knowledge is not tied to one fixed view.
plos-pone-0000990:
Natalia Komarova and Dominik Wodarz modeled how resting tumor cells affect leukemia therapy, in PLOS ONE in 2007. In chronic myelogenous leukemia, the most primitive cancer cells can enter quiescence, a state where they stop dividing for a time. Resting cells are hard for drugs to kill, since many therapies strike dividing cells.

Using mathematical models, the pair ask how that rest state changes the success of targeted treatment. A model can test schedules and combinations far faster than trials can. Their work helps explain why a therapy can clear most disease yet fail at the root. It also points to what a cure would have to handle.
plos-pone-0001090:
Martins Kalis, Per Leveen, Valeriya Lyssenko and colleagues linked variants in a fatty acid receptor gene to beta cell function, in PLOS ONE in 2007. The receptor FFAR1 sits mainly on pancreatic beta cells, the cells that release insulin. It is switched on by medium and long chain fatty acids and by a class of diabetes drugs, raising calcium and promoting insulin release.

Those properties make its gene a natural suspect in diabetes. The team report variants in FFAR1 are associated with beta cell function. A receptor that senses dietary fat and tunes insulin is a neat meeting point of food and hormone. The association supports FFAR1 as a drug target worth care.
plos-pone-0001190:
Influenza A viruses mutate constantly and swap gene segments, so new strains keep emerging from animal reservoirs, as the H5N1 bird flu virus did. A. T. Heiny and colleagues looked for the stable parts of the virus in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. They searched avian and human influenza A viruses for protein sequences that stay conserved through all that change.

Conserved sequences are attractive vaccine targets because a vaccine aimed at them might work against many strains, not just one. The authors present such sequences as candidate targets. Their approach addresses the central problem of flu vaccination: the target keeps moving.
plos-pone-0001290:
Violence is a leading cause of illness and death in South Africa. Katherine Doolan, Rodney Ehrlich, and Landon Myer examined how the experience of violence relates to socioeconomic position. Theirs was a national study, reported in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. Violence research usually treats social position as a confounder to control away; a social epidemiology approach treats it as part of the story.

The authors analyze who experiences violence across the social ladder in South Africa. Patterns by income, education, and employment shape where prevention should aim. Their national data give the public health approach to violence a firmer base.
plos-pone-0001390:
Marco Salemi and co-authors wrote a 2008 PLOS ONE study on HIV in Albania. In west Europe, one subtype of HIV-1 drives most cases. Far less was known about the east, where other subtypes are more common. AIDS cases in Albania had risen fast in the prior six years. The team set out to map the local strains.

Using close gene reads, they traced the types of HIV-1 found in Albania and their past. Their map shows how the virus spread and changed in the country. Such maps help health teams plan tests, care, and vaccines. They also show how a local epidemic can differ from the pattern next door.
plos-pone-0001490:
Eiji Goto and colleagues published a 2008 PLOS ONE methods paper on watching tagged proteins enter cells. When a surface protein is tagged for removal, it is pulled inside the cell. That step is hard to see as it happens in mammal cells. The gap blocked work on how tagging drives the pull in.

The team built a system that makes this step easy to track and rate. With it, labs can watch the pull in live and in bulk. A clear view should reveal the parts that run the process. That in turn may expose drug targets on paths that many receptors share.
plos-pone-0001590:
Francine Grodstein and co-authors wrote a 2008 PLOS ONE study on telomeres and dementia risk. Dementia takes decades to grow, so care must start early to have a chance. Marks that flag risk years ahead are thus prized. Telomeres, the caps on DNA ends, shrink with age and stress. The team ran a first check in 62 women from a large nurses' study.

Shorter telomeres went with higher early risk marks for dementia in this small set. The authors stress the work is a first look, not a verdict. Larger checks must test the link before any clinic use. Still, a cheap blood mark for dementia risk would be a major gain.
plos-pone-0001690:
Petter Minnhagen and Sebastian Bernhardsson questioned whether evolution shaped the layout of cell metabolism, in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Their model is called the blind watchmaker network. Metabolic networks, which map how a cell's chemistry links together, are scale-free: a few compounds take part in very many reactions, most in few.

The authors suggest this pattern reflects plain randomness, implying natural selection pressed little on the network's degree distribution during evolution. The full text gives the model, its math, and the match to real metabolic networks of simple organisms. If the layout is mostly chance, the search for adaptive design in network shape needs sharper tests. If not, the model marks where selection's hand should show.
plos-pone-0001790:
Marta Luisa Ciofi degli Atti, Stefano Merler, Caterina Rizzo, and their co-authors modeled pandemic influenza in Italy in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Models that simulate spread person to person can give the most reliable estimates for disease planning. The question was what various control measures would achieve in an Italian pandemic.

The team paired a global SEIR model for cases from abroad with a detailed national model. They then tracked the spread of pandemic flu under different scenarios. The full text gives the scenarios and the forecast case counts. Plans written before a pandemic decide school shutdowns and vaccine priorities under pressure, so tested models are a core planning tool.
plos-pone-0001890:
Fumiaki Sato and colleagues built a scoring tool for a throat condition that can turn to cancer, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. In Barrett esophagus, acid harm changes the lining of the food pipe, and a small share of cases move on to cancer. Watching all such patients closely is costly, and doctors did not agree on its worth.

The team sorted patients into three risk tiers using both health facts and chemical marks on DNA that can mute genes. A clear tier score helps doctors watch high-risk patients closely and spare low-risk ones needless tests. Work of this sort turns a vague worry into a plan with steps matched to risk.
plos-pone-0001990:
Nicholas Cothros, Jeremy Wong, and Paul Gribble tested how the brain learns to reach against odd forces, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. When people learn to move in a new force field, learning a second field often disrupts the first. A recent idea held that the brain treats such tasks as handling a novel object.

If so, a distinct feel in the hand, a haptic cue, might let the brain keep the two skills apart. As the title states, distinct cues did not reduce the interference. That null result trims a neat theory and pushes learning science toward other accounts of how skills collide.
plos-pone-0002090:
Shih-Hwa Chiou and co-authors found radiation-proof cells in a rare child brain tumor, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. Atypical teratoid/rhabdoid tumor is an extremely malignant tumor of the central nervous system that strikes infants and children. Recent work suggested that CD133 marks brain cancer stem-like cells, the seeds thought to regrow tumors.

The role of CD133 in this tumor was unclear. As the title states, the team identified CD133-positive cells that are radioresistant in these tumors. If a small seed set survives radiation, it may explain relapse, and it becomes the target that therapy must kill.
plos-pone-0002190:
Sonja Kleinlogel and Andrew White explored how shrimp see polarized light, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Animal eyes can detect brightness, color, and the direction of light waves, called polarization. Systems studied before theirs could sense up to four channels of linear polarization, paired against each other.

Mantis shrimps turned out to go further. The authors describe a visual system with a richer set of polarization channels than any known before. Such an eye can read patterns in light that are invisible to humans, and possibly to the shrimp's prey and rivals. The work marks one of the most advanced polarization vision systems found in nature.
plos-pone-0002290:
Keith Baverstock and Mauno Rönkkö wrote on how mammalian cells are regulated without changes to their DNA code, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Such epigenetic regulation decides which genes a cell uses to express its phenotype, its working form. Ionizing radiation can flip a normal cell into a genomic instability state, where copying the genome accurately becomes unreliable.

The authors set out a view of the mammalian cell as a regulated epigenetic system. In their account, that system, not DNA damage alone, explains how one radiation exposure can echo across many cell generations. The paper is a conceptual piece meant to reframe how instability after radiation is studied.
plos-pone-0002390:
Work from Yeka and fellow authors appeared in PLOS ONE in 2008. The byline credits Adoke Yeka, Grant Dorsey, Moses R. Kamya, and others. Its subject is artemether-Lumefantrine versus Dihydroartemisinin-Piperaquine for Treating Uncomplicated Malaria: A Randomized Trial to Guide Policy in Uganda. Uganda recently adopted artemether-lumefantrine (AL) as the recommended first-line treatment for uncomplicated malaria.

Key terms are set out in context, so a reader new to the field can still follow the work. The result is a compact record of the work, of use to readers who study the same problem or teach it to others. PLOS ONE is an open journal, and the full text can be read free by anyone who wants to check the work.
plos-pone-0002490:
